The halo fades; minorities often remain Reach of communities, growing with time Soft shading: the faith with the majority or largest following, by modern country (approximate) Mission, journey or campaign recorded in sources (gold Christian, green Muslim) Route known from tradition, or inferred from trade

    Soft shading marks areas where one faith held the majority or the largest following. It follows modern country outlines, so it is approximate in time and space. It fades in and out over about a century. Countries with large secular populations, such as those of northern Europe, keep the shading of their heritage faith. India, China, Japan and countries with no clear majority are left unshaded, as are areas that were mixed. Estimates before 1900 are informed approximations. Halos show where Christian or Muslim rule or an established community is attested. They accumulate over time. They do not show population share, denomination or sect, or the degree of conversion, and they are not state borders. A grey ring and a fading halo mark a place where rule or the main community ended, as in Iberia, Sicily, North Africa, Nubia, Central Asia and Japan. Minorities often continued there, and the map marks only the end of rule or of the principal community. Dates marked as tradition, including early Alexandria, Edessa, India and Arabia before 632, are approximate. Where a city belongs to both stories, the two pins sit side by side. Routes are schematic. Modern figures are from Pew Research Center (2025).
